records.name: Burkina Faso
records.summary_text:
Burkina Faso is dangerous for trans visitors. In July 2024 the military junta approved a revised Personal and Family Code criminalising homosexuality — Burkina Faso had never previously outlawed it. The junta (Traoré) has clamped down on opposition and media, promised elections have not been held, and much of the country faces jihadist insurgency. Enforcement details of the new law remain unclear (HDT notes drafting uncertainty), but the direction and the absence of any institutional recourse are unambiguous.

records.name: Mozambique
records.summary_text:
Mozambique demands real caution from trans visitors — one of Africa's better legal positions. Same-sex conduct was decriminalised under the 2015 Penal Code; courts ruled in 2017 that LGBTIQ organisations can register (Lambda Mozambique); and there is no documented pattern of police targeting. Counterweights: no legal gender recognition, no SOGI hate-crime statute, social hostility outside Maputo is significant, and the Cabo Delgado insurgency affects the north (a general, not trans-specific, risk).

For a visitor: no legal exposure; modest infrastructure; avoid the north.

records.name: Angola
records.summary_text:

records.name: Zambia
records.summary_text:
Zambia is dangerous for trans visitors. The Penal Code criminalises same-sex conduct (up to 14 years) with documented recent enforcement: Amnesty International's November 2024 campaign highlights Madalitso Zulu, serving a 15-year sentence with hard labour; Amnesty's 2024 regional report documents rising hostility in Zambia. There is no legal gender recognition, religious leaders lead anti-LGBT mobilisation, and police are perpetrators more than protectors.

For a visitor: visible trans presentation risks arrest; the documented serving-sentence case shows courts impose maximum terms.
